title: Madhyamaka — the middle way of emptiness
when: Madhyamaka took shape in India in the early centuries CE. Nāgārjuna, usually dated to about 150–250 CE, is its foundational philosopher, though details of his life and the attribution of some texts remain uncertain.
people: Nāgārjuna; Āryadeva, an early Madhyamaka thinker; later interpreters including Candrakīrti.
origin: Buddhist philosophical debates in ancient India, drawing on Mahāyāna Perfection of Wisdom literature. Madhyamaka later shaped Buddhist thought across Tibet, China, Japan, and elsewhere.
idea: Madhyamaka, or the Middle Way, argues that things are empty of svabhāva: an independent, self-grounding nature. A cart, person, or institution exists through parts, causes, relationships, and the concepts by which we identify it; none stands alone as an unchanging foundation. Emptiness does not mean that nothing exists. Rather, dependence makes ordinary things and causal action possible, while warning against treating our categories as ultimate. Nāgārjuna’s Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way examines how claims about causes, change, and identity become incoherent when their terms are imagined to exist independently. Madhyamaka also distinguishes everyday conventional truth from ultimate analysis, without turning emptiness itself into a new absolute substance.
relevance: The view invites scrutiny of assumptions that identities, institutions, or categories are fixed and self-sufficient. It can support intellectual humility and attention to relationships, while leaving room to distinguish more and less useful conventional accounts. Its challenge remains philosophical as well as practical: how can we reason and act responsibly if our descriptions are never final foundations?
